essay_title: Hostile Environments in Ann Radcliffe's The Romance of the Forest
special_features: Continuous prose with TWO internal subheadings: 'Limitations of Literary Darwinism and Cognitive Approaches to Literature' (PDF 87, book p.77) and 'Gibson's Affordances and the Humanities' (PDF 102, book p.92); third de-facto section 'The Romance of the Forest' begins at PDF 112, book p.102

outline: PDF 87 (book p.77) opens with the chapter thesis-in-miniature: environments, technically understood via J. J. Gibson, can make people 'terribly uncomfortable to the point of becoming unhinged. Or even "undone," as rape victim Antonia protests in Matthew Lewis's The Monk (1796) just before narrative logic finishes her off.' The 'undone' formula — Gross paraphrases Antonia's exclamation about completed ruin — names the diagnostic Gross extracts from Gothic-sentimental fiction: the genre studies precisely those cases where human environments (domestic 'scenes' and social institutions) themselves pose threats, not just nominal physical dangers. Gross stakes the chapter's claim that the model of cognition one adopts determines what one sees in literary representations of human environments, and that this issue is the load-bearing crux of any productive science-humanities encounter. Section 1 ('Limitations of Literary Darwinism and Cognitive Approaches to Literature,' PDF 87-101, book pp.77-91) is a polemical clearing of the ground: Brian Boyd's On the Origin of Stories (2009), Joseph Carroll, and Jonathan Gottschall (Evolution, Literature, and Film 2010) anchor Literary Darwinism (evocriticism); Lisa Zunshine (Why We Read Fiction 2006; Introduction to Cognitive Cultural Studies 2010) and Ellen Spolsky anchor Cognitive Approaches to Literature (CAL). Gross argues both movements smuggle in 'orthodox' Evolutionary Psychology (Cosmides, Tooby, Pinker, Buss) via three retreats — neuroplasticity, multilevel selection, gene-culture coevolution — that leave intact the basic move from biological universals to literary specifics. He catalogues two logical fallacies (affirming the consequent, the undistributed middle) and six 'red flags' (Pleistocene/hunter-gatherer; evolved mental architecture; consilience; modularity; neuron-talk; plasticity-as-black-box). Particular attention goes to Boyd's kin-selection extrapolation (Genesis to The Sopranos, PDF 88), to Zunshine's account of overcoming her boredom with Turgenev's nature passages by routing them through Theory of Mind (PDF 89-90), and to Elaine Scarry's Dreaming by the Book (1999), which Gross treats as the unassimilated good case — Scarry uses Gibson on kinetic occlusion and perceptual acuity to argue that narrative (e.g., Tess of the d'Urbervilles' opening, where the reader is instructed to look at the walker's legs) imitates perceptual cognition rather than activating it (PDF 90-91). Lakoff is registered against Gibson on cultural variability of emotional affordances (anger as inflammatory by local laws and 'injurable people'). The section closes (PDF 101-102) anticipating three nested levels of environment-analysis — biologically dangerous, legally hostile (workplace), and rhetorically hostile (Gothic-fictional). Section 2 ('Gibson's Affordances and the Humanities,' PDF 102-111, book pp.92-101) constructs the chapter's positive theoretical apparatus. Andrea Scarantino's 2003 Philosophy of Science definition gives Gross the symmetric scaffold: 'affordances of the environment ... are the offerings of the environment, roughly the sets of threats (negative affordances) and promises (positive affordances) that characterize items in the environment relative to organisms.' Gross bridges directly to Aristotle Rhet. II — Cydias on Samos (1384b32-35), the 'tribunal of conscience' rhetorical figure, is read as the archetypal negative affordance: a threat constituted by storytelling rather than by physical danger. Lloyd Bitzer's 1968 'rhetorical situation' (exigence/audience/constraints) is rehabilitated as proto-affordance theory; the chapter's signature case follows at PDF 104-105 (book pp.94-95): the cop-car roof on which Mario Savio stood on UC Berkeley campus October 1, 1964, on behalf of Free Speech Movement organizer Jack Weinberg. The roof is climb-up-able in Gibson's invariant sense, but once the event entered the historical record it became 'always there to be perceived' as a stage-for-speaking-persuasively — variable as a perceptual fact, fixed as a rhetorical-historical one. Cop car roofs in certain circumstances now say 'plead on me' or 'harangue on me.' Gross multiplies the case to open mics, the US Senate podium, coffee-house stages — items hailing loudly from the social or cultural world (PDF 105). The chapter then distinguishes two analytic registers within the post-Gibsonian frame (PDF 105): cultural environments (communication-structures like myths and rituals — Aufforderungscharakter from Lewin and Koffka) vs. social environments (organizational structures like stratification). Gestalt psychology is reconstructed at PDF 104 via Koffka's Principles ('a fruit says Eat me; water says Drink me; thunder says Fear me; and woman says Love me'), Kurt Lewin's A Dynamic Theory of Personality (1935) with its Aufforderungscharakter / valence / Umweltkrafte / Umstrukturierung / Aus-dem-Felde-Gehen lexicon, Jakob von Uexkull's Umwelt cited via Lewin, and Erik Rietveld's Wittgensteinian reformulation of expert-craftsman responsiveness. Lewin's 'hopeless situation' (1935, p.94) — the child who, finding the environment wholly disagreeable, contracts physically and psychically and 'encysts' the self — becomes Gross's load-bearing concept for what Adeline confronts later. PDF 108 introduces the legal hostile-work-environment case: AT&T's $5M settlement to a Muslim Kansas City employee, where the workplace is defined as a niche of culturally-specific affordances activated by counterfactual standards ('could have known, should have known'). Gibson's Shannon-Weaver-derived theory of language and communication is critiqued (PDF 107, Fig. 3.1) as the 'positivist back door' through which mind/body dualism re-enters Gibson's own monism; language for Gibson, Gross notes, is 'a different kind of knowledge' that bumps awkwardly against the rhetorical situation Cydias inhabits. Scarantino's typology of physical, mental, nonbasic-physical, and language-mediated affordances (Philosophy of Science 2003) is reviewed (PDF 109) and judged still insufficient: Aristotle's negative-affordance-as-damaged-reputation is rhetorical, neither physical nor mental but transactive across them. The section closes (PDF 110-111) gesturing forward: Pinker, Dutton, Tooby-Cosmides on Pleistocene savanna preference are flagged as evocritical mis-steps that go where Gibson would not follow; Radcliffe is then introduced — via David Herman's tag — as an Umwelt researcher whose fiction 'optimizes the study of hostility because it tells the story with the right social and organic facts.' Section 3 ('The Romance of the Forest,' PDF 112-120, book pp.102-110) is the literary reading. Gross begins with the Oxford World's Classics back cover description — Adeline, mysteriously placed under the protection of the La Motte family fleeing Paris for debt, finds refuge in a ruined abbey in south-eastern France with a skeleton, manuscript, and rusty dagger concealed in inner rooms (Fig. 3.2 reproduces Constable's c.1833 Netley Abbey). The chapter-2 abbey-arrival passage (Radcliffe pp.14-15) is paraphrased: La Motte 'perceives' the 'Gothic remains of an Abbey' — once 'the pride of monkish devotion' — half-ruined, half-residence-of-birds-of-prey, lawn-overshadowed by 'high and spreading trees,' suspended in 'romantic gloom.' Gross treats this passage as a tutorial in trans-species affordance mutuality: counterfactual structures ('plausibly the abbey could be this and it could be that'), free-indirect-discourse environmental qualities ('gloomily romantic' to whom?), and the genre-defining co-constitution of threatening creatures with the environment they inhabit (replace 'birds of prey' with 'giant snails' and the genre changes). Adeline at p.34 is shown 'overlooking' the abbey, recoding its terrific aspect as a 'domestic asylum, and a safe refuge from the storms of power' — the affordance varies precisely as her character-quality 'exactness' is exercised. PDF 116 (book p.105) launches the keyword 'asylum' — granted by powers that be and subject to them, it is never an absolute security; self-deception ('let me still be deceived,' p.150) becomes the basic condition of trust under Gothic-epistemological uncertainty. The Marquis de Montalt is introduced (PDF 116-117, book pp.105-106) as the lawful owner of the Abbey, whose offer of 'honorable asylum' (p.125) is the chapter's paradigm of promise=threat affordance: rhetorically structured, ironically delivered, abused by power. Walter Scott's 'supernatural explained' formula is contested: Radcliffe's transitions, Gross argues, do not disenchant in the post-Enlightenment manner but route the supernatural as spectral — 'slipping through our fingers and evading our glances, just out of earshot' — at the very moment of its concrete threat (PDF 117-118, citing Adeline's manuscript scene, Radcliffe p.134). Paradiastole (re-description) is identified as Radcliffe's signature rhetorical figure at PDF 119: La Motte chooses not to abandon Adeline to 'the care, or rather, to the neglect, of strangers' (p.12); the Lady Abbess 'denounces and terrifies rather than persuades and allures' (p.36). Austin's perlocutionary/illocutionary distinction is invoked to render Gibson's direct/indirect distinction in rhetorical terms — threats and promises in human environments operate at the perlocutionary level where context can invert literal meaning. The social spectrum of the novel is mapped (PDF 120, book p.108): Peter (domestic, 'curiosity more prevalent than fear') and Annette retreat from the world that matters (Aus-dem-Felde-Gehen); the Marquis stands at the opposite social extreme, fearless and consequential; the surgeon botches Theodore's treatment with idealized indifference to circumstance ('My mind is not of that frivolous kind to be affected by circumstances,' p.186); Madame La Motte's husband is obligated to the Marquis 'whose territory afforded him a shelter from the world' but also empowered the Marquis 'to betray him into the hands of his enemies' (p.210) — Lewin's Umweltkrafte. Religious sensibility (PDF 121, book p.109) extends the affordance grid into secular/non-secular: Adeline's open-window prayer to the 'great Author of Nature' (p.22), La Luc's Burnet-derived theo-geology (Telluris Theoria Sacra 1694, flagged in Chloe Chard's Oxford notes), and the As You Like It II.1.3-7 'penalty of Adam' intertext that frames external nature as obscurely scripted. The Marquis's suicide and the king's justice (PDF 122, book p.110) close the narrative as an Umstrukturierung — Lewinian transformation of the total field. The chapter's last paragraph (PDF 122, book p.110) collapses into thesis: hostile work environments need legal research; but for other human environments — hostile, romantic, awkward, thrilling — the ecological concerns of natural and social scientists 'might in fact find their most inviting home in the wilds of literature.'

concepts.name: hostile environment
concepts.definition: Titular concept; an environment whose affordances are constitutively negative-but-not-merely-dangerous, requiring rhetorical/narrative analysis beyond physical risk. Three nested levels Gross distinguishes: (1) species-dangerous (e.g., coal mine), (2) legally-hostile (workplace per protected-class law), (3) rhetorically-hostile (Gothic-novel hostility a la Radcliffe).

concepts.name: Gibsonian affordance
concepts.definition: J. J. Gibson's (Ecological Approach to Visual Perception, 1979) invariant offerings of an environment to an organism relative to its action capacities; positive affordances (promises) and negative affordances (threats).

concepts.name: negative affordance / rhetorical affordance
concepts.definition: Gross's extension of Gibson: an environmental offering whose threat-character is constituted not by direct perception but by language- and narrative-mediated rhetorical situations (Aristotle's damaged-reputation tribunal, the cop-car roof as harangue-stage).

concepts.name: cop-car-roof affordance
concepts.definition: Gross's paradigmatic case (PDF 104-105, book pp.94-95) of historically-fixed rhetorical affordance: Mario Savio's 1964 use of a UC Berkeley campus cop car as speaking platform makes cop-car roofs in certain circumstances 'plead on me' / 'harangue on me' — climb-up-able as invariant physical affordance, speak-from-able as variable cultural affordance.

concepts.name: cultural vs. social affordance distinction
concepts.definition: Gross's bifurcation (PDF 105, book p.95) of the rhetorical affordance into cultural (myths, rituals, communication structures) and social (organizational, stratificatory structures) registers.

concepts.name: Gothic sentimental subgenre
concepts.definition: Genre Gross identifies (PDF 87) — Walpole, Lewis, Radcliffe — where the cause of death and the terms of a life-undone find their genre because emotional scenes can pose real threat. Gothic foregrounds asylum/dependence/epistemic-uncertainty as affordance structures.

concepts.name: 'undone' diagnostic
concepts.definition: Antonia's exclamation in Lewis The Monk (PDF 87) — a marker that the terms of a life have been undone, used by Gross as the chapter's emotional-rhetorical thesis-statement-in-miniature. NOT to be quoted at length per content-filter discipline.

concepts.name: Lewin's hopeless situation
concepts.definition: From Lewin A Dynamic Theory of Personality (1935, p.94): a wholly disagreeable inescapable situation in which the child contracts physically and psychically, builds a wall, and 'encysts' the self. Gross applies this to Adeline's predicament with the Marquis (PDF 116, book p.106) — 'we are encompassed with dangers,' resources foreclosed.

concepts.name: Aufforderungscharakter / valence
concepts.definition: Kurt Lewin's Gestalt-psychological term (translated invitation-character by Brown 1929, valence by Adams 1931) for the imperative-environmental fact that determines behavioral direction; Gibson derives 'affordance' from this lineage (PDF 104).

concepts.name: Umstrukturierung
concepts.definition: Lewinian transformation of the total field (PDF 105, recurring PDF 122) — Gross uses it for Radcliffe's narrative resolution (Marquis's suicide, king's justice) as field-transformation.

concepts.name: Aus-dem-Felde-Gehen
concepts.definition: Lewinian 'leaving the field' — embarrassment followed by withdrawal (PDF 105); Gross applies this to Peter and Annette, the domestics in Romance of the Forest who retreat from the world that matters (PDF 120, book p.108).

concepts.name: Umweltkrafte
concepts.definition: Lewinian fields of force; Gross uses it for the Marquis's hold over La Motte's husband — territory 'afforded him a shelter' yet empowered the Marquis to betray him (PDF 120, book p.108, Radcliffe p.210).

concepts.name: Umwelt (Uexkull-Lewin-Herman)
concepts.definition: Jakob von Uexkull's biological environment; cited via Lewin (PDF 105) and David Herman (PDF 111). Radcliffe is Gross's chosen Umwelt researcher in the literary mode.

concepts.name: rhetorical situation (Bitzer)
concepts.definition: Lloyd F. Bitzer 1968 — exigence, audience, constraints. Gross rehabilitates Bitzer as proto-affordance-theory (PDF 103) by re-reading Jack Weinberg's police-car arrest and the Free Speech Movement audience constituted by Savio's speech.

concepts.name: exigence / recalcitrance
concepts.definition: Bitzer's exigence as imperfection-marked-by-urgency; Kenneth Burke's earlier 'recalcitrance' (Permanence and Change, 1930s) is the prior analogue (chapter note 19, PDF Notes 832).

concepts.name: asylum (ironic)
concepts.definition: Radcliffe's keyword that Gross reads as the chapter's most concentrated promise=threat affordance. Marquis de Montalt offers 'honorable asylum' (Radcliffe p.125) — abuse of power inverts the affordance (PDF 116-117).

concepts.name: paradiastole (redescription)
concepts.definition: Rhetorical figure — naming a vice as a virtue or vice-versa by redescription. Gross identifies it as Radcliffe's signature trope (PDF 119): 'care, or rather, the neglect, of strangers' (p.12); 'denounce and terrify' instead of 'persuade and allure' (p.36).

concepts.name: perlocutionary vs. illocutionary (Austin)
concepts.definition: Austin's distinction invoked (PDF 119) to translate Gibson's direct/indirect divide into rhetorical terms — human-environmental threats and promises operate perlocutionarily, where context can invert literal sense ('be comforted'/'comfortable' as terror-renewal at Radcliffe p.7).

concepts.name: supernatural explained (Scott) — contested
concepts.definition: Walter Scott's claim that Radcliffe's seemingly supernatural events resolve naturally; Gross contests (PDF 117-118) — Radcliffe's transitions handle the supernatural as spectral residue, not as Enlightenment disenchantment.

concepts.name: mutuality of animal and environment
concepts.definition: Gibson's principle (Ecological Approach, p.8) that organism and environment co-constitute affordances; Gross uses it (PDF 114, book p.104) to argue trans-species mutuality is precisely what Gothic captures — replace 'birds of prey' with 'giant snails' and the abbey-environment changes genre.

concepts.name: hostile workplace (legal category)
concepts.definition: Legal niche defined by culturally-specific protected-class hostilities (race, age over 40, ability, religion); actionable via counterfactuals (could-have-known/should-have-known). AT&T Muslim-employee case, $5M, Kansas City (PDF 108).

concepts.name: Gibsonian monism (defended)
concepts.definition: Gibson's principle (Ecological Approach, p.130) that nature and artifice are one environment, not two. Gross honors this monism even while critiquing Gibson's positivist communication-theory (PDF 107).

concepts.name: Scarantino's affordance taxonomy
concepts.definition: Andrea Scarantino (Philosophy of Science 70, 2003) — basic physical, nonbasic physical, mental, language-mediated affordances. Gross judges still insufficient for the rhetorical affordance (PDF 109).

concepts.name: Theory of Mind (Zunshine) — contested
concepts.definition: Zunshine's cognitive-universal of mind-reading; Gross argues (PDF 89) ToM is less a universal than a particular bourgeois-novel reading-disposition (cf. Deidre Shauna Lynch). Zunshine's Turgenev-nature-passage anecdote (PDF 89) becomes Gross's exhibit A.

concepts.name: evocriticism / Literary Darwinism
concepts.definition: Brian Boyd's term for the application of evolutionary theory to literary criticism; Gross uses Boyd (Origin of Stories, 2009) as the chapter's primary foil and identifies the affirming-the-consequent fallacy at the core of consilience-arguments (PDF 92-93).

concepts.name: six red flags of biology-literature criticism
concepts.definition: Gross's enumeration (PDF 93): Pleistocene/hunter-gatherer (remote); evolved mind / evolved mental architecture (question-begging); consilience (reductive); modularity (deterministic); neuron (too small); plasticity (black box, too big).

concepts.name: Scarry on Gibson + narrative-as-perceptual-imitation
concepts.definition: Elaine Scarry (Dreaming by the Book, 1999) — narrative imitates rather than activates perceptual cognition (Tess of the d'Urbervilles' opening as series of erased imperatives). Gross's good case for Gibson-humanities bridge (PDF 90-91).

concepts.name: Lakoff's cultural-cognitive emotion
concepts.definition: George Lakoff — anger as cognitive but culturally-defined, varying by local laws and 'injurable people'; thus emotional affordances are not invariant. Gross's bridge between Gibson and rhetorical-affordance (PDF 91).

concepts.name: Adeline as overlooker
concepts.definition: Radcliffe's heroine — initially terror-struck by the abbey, recodes it as 'domestic asylum' (Radcliffe p.34), exercises 'admirable exactness' in 'overlooking little affairs of the household.' Gross's figure for character-quality emerging only in environmental relation.

concepts.name: Marquis de Montalt as Gothic predator
concepts.definition: Lawful owner of the abbey; offerer of 'honorable asylum'; emotional-political center of the novel — emotional life 'may not be recognizable to someone of the middling sort, at the same time that it is deeply consequential' (PDF 120, book p.108, Radcliffe p.202).

concepts.name: self-deception (Gothic-epistemic)
concepts.definition: 'Let me still be deceived' — Adeline at Radcliffe p.150; Gross reads self-deception as the basic condition of trust-and-well-being under Gothic epistemic uncertainty (PDF 116, book p.105).

concepts.name: Gilpin picturesque (1788)
concepts.definition: William Gilpin Observations Relative Chiefly to Picturesque Beauty (1788) — the contemporaneous aesthetic theorist who 'naturalizes' the ruins of abbeys into landscape. Gross uses Gilpin (PDF 113) to frame Radcliffe's abbey as picturesque-affordance.

concepts.name: Burnet's Telluris Theoria Sacra (1694) — theo-geology
concepts.definition: Thomas Burnet's theory that mountains are post-Flood ruins of previous natural formations; flagged in Chloe Chard's Oxford World's Classics notes (Radcliffe p.390n265) and reactivated by Gross to articulate Radcliffe's religious-naturalistic register (PDF 121, book p.109).

concepts.name: penalty-of-Adam intertext
concepts.definition: Radcliffe's epigraph to ch.3 quotes As You Like It II.1.3-7 ('here feel we but the penalty of Adam') — Gross uses this Shakespearean source to register external-nature-as-obscurely-scripted (PDF 121, book p.109).

concepts.name: supernatural-as-spectral (vs. supernatural-explained)
concepts.definition: Radcliffe's transitional handling of the supernatural — slipping through fingers, evading glances, just out of earshot, while threatening concretely; not Scott's 'supernatural explained' (PDF 117-118).

concepts.name: Shannon-Weaver mathematical theory of communication (1949) — critique
concepts.definition: Gross's diagnosis (PDF 107-108, Fig. 3.1) — Gibson's residual mid-century positivism leans on Shannon-Weaver, importing mind/body dualism through the back door despite Gibson's monism.

concepts.name: affirming-the-consequent fallacy in CAL/evocriticism
concepts.definition: Gross's logical critique of Boyd (PDF 91): 'if biocultural P then take-evolution-seriously Q; Q therefore P' is invalid. Even granted that evolution shapes minds, no commitment to biocultural literary criticism follows.

concepts.name: undistributed middle fallacy (evocriticism)
concepts.definition: Gross's second logical critique (PDF 96) — attention/imagination/cognition/emotion are deeply explored via evolved-cultural human nature, BUT not every category that engages these is best explored that way.

concepts.name: ingroup-outgroup hostility (evocritical thin)
concepts.definition: Sterelny Thought in a Hostile World (2003); Hogan on 'literary universals' of in-group jokes. Gross grants evolutionary-psychology's purchase here but argues it cannot say much of interest about hostile workplaces, let alone Radcliffean hostile environments (PDF 110, note 27-28).

concepts.name: Pleistocene-savanna-preference (rejected)
concepts.definition: Orians-Heerwagen, Pinker, Dutton — the evocritical claim that landscape aesthetics reveal Pleistocene habitat-choice. Gross flags this as where evocriticism abandons Gibson (PDF 110-111).

concepts.name: Rietveld on Wittgenstein expert craftsman
concepts.definition: Erik Rietveld (Mind 117, 2008) — expert craftsman 'allows himself to be moved by the situation,' perceives a relevant solicitation to act. Gross uses Rietveld (PDF 106) to extend Gibson into culturally-trained perception, with the affective dimension of 'discontent, disgust, and discomfort' (Wittgenstein Lectures on Aesthetics 1938).

concepts.name: ecological-rhetorical theory (Gross's coinage)
concepts.definition: The chapter's positive theoretical product — a theory of human environments where Gibsonian ecology, Gestalt-psychological valence, Bitzerian rhetorical situation, and literary Umwelt-research combine. Cross-pipeline kin to Rickert's Ambient Rhetoric.

positions.claim: J. J. Gibson's affordance theory can and must be extended into a rhetorical-historical-cultural theory of negative/hostile affordances, against the prevailing orthodox ecological-psychology reading that holds affordances strictly invariant and pre-linguistic.
positions.support: Cop-car-roof case (PDF 104-105); Aristotle's Cydias on Samos as negative affordance (PDF 102-103); Lewin's Aufforderungscharakter genealogy (PDF 104-105); legal hostile-work-environment case (PDF 108).
positions.contested_by: Orthodox Gibsonian ecological psychology; Scarantino's narrower taxonomy of affordances (PDF 109).

positions.claim: Gothic-sentimental fiction (Walpole, Lewis, Radcliffe) provides the literary-research laboratory in which hostile environments are most fully described — not because the genre is realistic but because its narrative form captures the trans-species and trans-rhetorical mutualities that science and social science cannot reach.
positions.support: Radcliffe Romance of the Forest abbey-scene reading (PDF 113-114); the 'overlooks' / 'asylum' / paradiastole machinery (PDF 114-119); David Herman's invocation of Radcliffe as Umwelt researcher (PDF 111).
positions.contested_by: Literary Darwinism (Boyd); CAL/Zunshine; evolutionary-psychology readings that treat literature as projection or adaptation.

positions.claim: Affordances in human environments must be analyzed at TWO distinct registers — cultural (communication-structural; myths, rituals) and social (organizational; stratification) — and these are NOT reducible to one another.
positions.support: Explicit articulation at PDF 105: 'the relevant patterns reside substantially in an environment we call cultural or social, depending upon the analytic frame.' Kitayama-Mesquita-Karasawa 2006 (cultural affordances) + Kaufman-Clement 2007 (social affordances) cited in notes 20-21.
positions.contested_by: Reductive consilience programs (E. O. Wilson; Pinker) that collapse cultural to social and both to biological.

positions.claim: Literary Darwinism and Cognitive Approaches to Literature share the same core logical failure: they smuggle in orthodox Evolutionary Psychology through the rhetorical maneuvers of affirming-the-consequent and the undistributed middle.
positions.support: Detailed formal critique at PDF 91 and PDF 96; specific cases include Boyd's kin-selection-to-Sopranos leap (PDF 88), Zunshine's ToM-as-universal claim (PDF 89-90).
positions.contested_by: Boyd, Zunshine, Spolsky, Carroll, Gottschall (the named principals).

positions.claim: Rhetorical situations are themselves a species of affordance — Bitzer's exigence/audience/constraints is proto-affordance-theory, and Aristotle's Rhetoric II is the earliest negative-affordance treatise.
positions.support: Aristotle Rhet. 1384b32-35 (Cydias on Samos) reading (PDF 102-103); Bitzer's 1968 essay rehabilitated as proto-Gibson (PDF 103); Mario Savio as Bitzer-exigence-audience-constraint diagram (PDF 103, drawing on Jack Weinberg arrest).
positions.contested_by: Strict Gibsonians who reject any linguistic-rhetorical extension of affordance.

positions.claim: Walter Scott's 'supernatural explained' formula misreads Radcliffe — her transitional handling of the seemingly supernatural is NOT disenchantment but rather a spectral-residue technique where threats slip through fingers, evade glances, and remain just-out-of-earshot at the same moment they threaten most concretely.
positions.support: Manuscript-reading scene (Radcliffe p.134) — 'Holy Virgin, protect me'/'transient gleam of peace'/'appearance of the Marquis' sequence (PDF 117-118); Adeline's prayer at open window (Radcliffe p.22, PDF 121).
positions.contested_by: Walter Scott Lives of Novelists (1825); broad post-Enlightenment-disenchantment reading of Gothic.

tensions.description: Gibson holds that affordances are 'always there to be perceived' regardless of need/perception. Gross argues the cop-car-roof becomes a speaking-platform affordance only after Mario Savio (Oct 1 1964) — historically fixed but not pre-historically invariant. Both invariance and variance must obtain at different analytic levels.

tensions.axis: Gibson monism vs. Gibson positivist-Shannon-Weaver communication theory
tensions.description: Gibson asserts (p.130) a monism that refuses to separate natural from artificial environments. Yet Gibson's own theory of language and communication (composed via Shannon-Weaver 1949) reimports mind/body dualism through the back door — language is 'a different kind of knowledge,' secondhand. Gross honors monism while critiquing the positivist residue.

Gross's explicit bifurcation at PDF 105. The same cop-car roof can be analyzed culturally (as myth-ritual-communication item: 'plead on me') or socially (as organizational fact: 'this stratum of the campus uses cars-as-platforms'). The two analytics produce different findings, neither reducible to the other.

Scott's reading domesticates Radcliffe's Gothic into Enlightenment disenchantment ('on natural principles at the winding up of the story'). Gross argues Radcliffe's transitional handling sustains spectrality — the supernatural slips through fingers, evades glances, just out of earshot, at the very moment of concrete threat.

tensions.axis: Evocriticism/CAL universal vs. domain-specific critical theory
tensions.description: Boyd-Zunshine claim cognitive-architecture/Theory-of-Mind universals can host culturally-historically-specific literary criticism additively. Gross argues the universals always dominate the weighting (PDF 88) — the result is reductive consilience under polite cover.

tensions.axis: Adeline's 'domestic asylum' vs. abbey as 'potential slaughterhouse'
tensions.description: Radcliffe's narrative provides simultaneous, irreconcilable affordance-redescriptions of the same physical structure depending on the situational frame: Adeline's domestic-asylum recoding at p.34 vs. the abbey-as-slaughterhouse formulation at p.338. The character-environment relation is constitutively dialectical.

tensions.axis: Gibson's prelinguistic perception vs. Aristotle's tribunal-of-conscience
tensions.description: Gibson's theory is adamantly prelinguistic and pre-cultural; Aristotle's Cydias case constitutes the threat (damaged reputation) purely through storytelling/imagination of the Greek polities. The two cannot both be the level at which the affordance lives.

'Honorable asylum' (Radcliffe p.125) is offered as protection; in the rhetorical situation it is a coercive predation. Promise=threat. The 'rhetoric of affordances' is precisely this inversion — and it cannot be analyzed at the level of direct perception.

cross_pipeline_bridges.anchor: Gross's negative-affordance/rhetorical-affordance extension is the 2017 application of the 2005 rhetorical-ontology thesis to environment-theory. The cop-car-roof case operationalizes what HR-01-GROSS s2 argued abstractly — that rhetorical situations have ontic weight independent of immediate perception.

Strongest cross-pipeline bridge: Rickert's ambient/attunement/kairos-as-situated extends rhetorical-situation theory beyond Bitzer in precisely the direction Gross extends Gibson — both turn rhetorical analysis toward the agential environment. Rickert is named in Acknowledgments. The cop-car-roof's 'plead on me' is a Rickertian attunement-fact.

Cydias on Samos at Rhet. 1384b32-35 is Gross's direct anchor; the chapter argues that Aristotle's rhetoric ALREADY is an affordance theory of human-environmental threats and promises (damaged reputation as primary negative affordance).
